q: In which country is the city of Basel, the seat of the Bank for International Settlements, located?
explain: Basel is a Swiss city and the headquarters of the BIS.

q: What is the full form of BCBS?
explain: BCBS is the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which frames the Basel accords.

q: What is the main purpose of the Basel accords?
options: To ensure banks hold enough capital to meet obligations and absorb unexpected losses
To fix the repo rate for all countries
To set exchange rates between currencies
explain: The accords mainly address risks to banks and the financial system by requiring adequate capital.

q: The first Basel Concordat was concerned with
options: The division of supervisory responsibilities among national authorities
explain: The 1975 Concordat dealt with who supervises what among national authorities; capital rules came with Basel I in 1988.

q: Which of these is the risk of losses on on-balance sheet and off-balance sheet positions arising from movements in market prices?
explain: Market risk covers losses from price movements. Credit risk is about borrower default.

q: In which year did the BCBS introduce the Basel I capital accord?
explain: Basel I came in 1988; Basel II in 2004; Basel III in 2010.

q: What minimum capital requirement did Basel I fix?
explain: Basel I set capital at 8% of RWA.

q: Basel I mainly focused on which risk?
explain: Basel I focused almost entirely on credit risk and defined capital and the structure of risk weights.

q: Why does a collateral-backed loan carry a lower risk weight than an unsecured personal loan?
options: It is always free of interest
It is guaranteed by the RBI
It is given only to the government
Collateral reduces the loss if the borrower defaults
explain: Risk weighted assets give different weights to assets with different risk profiles.

q: In which year were the Basel II guidelines published by the BCBS?
explain: Basel II was published in 2004 as a refined and reformed version of Basel I.

q: Which of these was NOT one of the three parameters of Basel II?
options: Minimum capital adequacy of 8% of risk assets
explain: The liquidity ratios belong to Basel III. Basel II covered capital, risk management and disclosure.

q: In India the Basel II minimum capital adequacy practice is equivalent to maintaining
explain: CAR is the Indian version of capital against risk-weighted assets; CRR and SLR are reserve requirements.

q: What does the Basel II disclosure requirement aim to raise?
options: Confidence of investors and depositors in the bank
explain: More transparent banks are deemed more stable, which raises confidence.

q: Which Basel II pillar deals with market discipline through disclosure?
explain: Pillar 1 is minimum capital, Pillar 2 supervisory review and Pillar 3 market discipline.

q: How often does the RBI publish its Financial Stability Report, as mentioned in the study material?
explain: The RBI publishes the Financial Stability Report bi-annually.

q: The Basel III guidelines were introduced in response to which event?
explain: Basel III came in 2010 after the 2008 global financial crisis.

q: Basel III capital regulations were released by the BCBS as a global regulatory framework in
explain: The BCBS released Basel III in December 2010; RBI’s own guidelines followed on 2 May 2012.

q: On which date did the RBI release its guidelines on Basel III capital regulation?
explain: RBI released the guidelines on 2 May 2012; implementation began on 1 April 2013.

q: As per the Basel III implementation in India, minimum Tier 1 capital must be what percent of risk weighted assets on an ongoing basis?
explain: Tier 1 must be at least 7%, while total capital (Tier 1 + Tier 2) must be at least 9%.

q: What is the minimum total capital ratio (Tier 1 plus Tier 2) under the RBI’s Basel III guidelines?
explain: RBI set total capital at 9% of RWA and Tier 1 at 7%.

q: Under Basel III the common equity requirement rose to 4.5% from what level under Basel II?
explain: Common equity was raised from 2% to 4.5%, more than doubling the requirement.

q: What does leverage mean in banking?
options: Holding extra cash in the vault
Buying assets with borrowed money to multiply gains
explain: Leverage is risky, so Basel III puts a limit on it.

q: The collapse of which institution is cited as an example of a run-like liquidity failure behind the 2008 recession?
explain: Lehman Brothers’ failure triggered the 2008 recession and showed why banks need liquid assets.

q: In India, the Basel III liquid-asset practice can be correlated with maintaining
explain: CRR and SLR are the Indian forms of keeping liquid assets with the central bank and in securities.

q: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is built around which time horizon?
explain: LCR covers a 30-day stress. The Net Stable Funding Ratio looks at one year.

q: The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) looks at funding stability over which horizon?
explain: NSFR covers a one-year horizon, unlike the 30-day LCR.

q: What is the capital conservation buffer under Basel III in India?
explain: The capital conservation buffer is an extra 2.5% cushion on top of minimum capital.

q: From which date did the RBI implement the Basel III recommendations in India?
explain: RBI began Basel III implementation on 1 April 2013 in phases.

q: Which group of banks depends mostly on the Government for raising extra capital under Basel III?
explain: Private banks can raise capital from markets; PSBs rely largely on government infusion.

q: Why may the higher liquid-asset requirement of Basel III reduce a bank’s operating profit margin?
options: Liquid assets are illegal to hold
Liquid assets usually give low returns
Liquid assets raise loan interest rates
explain: Banks must hold more low-yielding liquid assets, which can also crowd out private investment.

q: Which of these is NOT a challenge listed for implementing Basel III in India?
explain: Basel III raises capital needs; the challenges are capital, technology and liquidity.

q: The implementation date of the Basel III standards finalised in December 2017 was deferred by one year to
explain: The BCBS’s GHOS deferred it by a year because of the coronavirus pandemic.

q: The transitional arrangements for the output floor were extended to
explain: The output floor transition was also extended by one year, to 1 January 2028.

q: What does GHOS stand for in the Basel framework?
options: Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision
Group of Home Offices of Supervisors
explain: GHOS is the oversight body of the Basel Committee.

q: Which event led the Basel Committee to defer implementation of the Basel III standards in 2020?
options: A change in the BCBS membership
explain: The pandemic prompted a one-year deferral of the scheduled January 2022 start.
